Synthetic prospective nurse note. No real patient data.

The driver attends a commercial vehicle review after a change from local deliveries to overnight heavy-vehicle work. The GP record contains seated readings of 169/99 mmHg ten days ago and 172/102 mmHg four days ago. Today the nurse records 170/100 mmHg after five minutes seated and 170/100 mmHg again after a further ten minutes with an appropriately sized cuff. The driver describes a dull headache after a night shift but no chest pain, focal weakness or visual disturbance. The medication list shows a new antihypertensive started three days ago; the GP has not yet documented a sustained response. His father had a stroke in his seventies.

Unaided distance acuity is 6/6 in each eye. An optometry report from last month records a binocular horizontal field of 150 degrees, no field defect, no diplopia and vision in both eyes. Clinical hearing assessment today records no suspected hearing loss, and ordinary instructions are followed without repetition. The driver denies any personal episode of collapse, loss of awareness or unexplained inability to recall a journey. There is no documented diabetes diagnosis or glucose-lowering medication. A recent routine glucose result is 5.3 mmol/L. The employer's form from a year ago contains the words 'blood pressure satisfactory', without a measurement or the name of the person who completed it.

Synthetic prospective nurse note. No real patient data.

The driver arrives directly after unloading freight and climbing two flights of stairs. A reception-machine printout shows 183/106 mmHg, but no rest period or cuff size is recorded. After fifteen minutes seated, the nurse measures 164/96 mmHg and then 168/98 mmHg. The home-monitor diary for the preceding fortnight lists values between 128/78 and 142/86, although the device has not been compared with a clinic instrument. The GP has asked for ambulatory monitoring; that appointment is next week. A discharge note six years ago mentioned an elevated blood pressure during an acute painful illness. No current antihypertensive appears on the reconciled medication list.

The driver reports no recent headache, chest pain, breathlessness or fainting. He mentions that his mother uses insulin; he has never been prescribed insulin or another diabetes treatment himself, and his GP records no diabetes diagnosis. Acuity measured with spectacles is 6/6 right and 6/6 left; the unaided figures were not entered on today's card. Last year's eye report records no diplopia and a binocular field of 150 degrees. A nurse's clinical hearing assessment is recorded as normal without an audiogram. The driver denies a personal history of spontaneous loss of consciousness. He brings an employer clearance signed before the monitoring referral, but the clearance contains no blood pressure data.

During a commercial-driver review, the driver hands over two eye cards. Today's optometry card records unaided distance acuity of 6/9 in the right eye and 6/12 in the left; with current spectacles the measurements are 6/6 in both eyes. A card dated eighteen months earlier shows unaided 6/6 in both eyes. The driver says the older card was copied into the employer's electronic form yesterday. The current optometrist records a binocular horizontal visual field of 140 degrees on formal testing, no confirmed focal field defect, no diplopia and no monocular loss of vision. The driver has not yet discussed the new test with an ophthalmologist.

The driver reports occasional glare when approaching low evening sunlight, but no sudden dark curtain, eye pain or transient loss of consciousness. Blood pressure after rest is 132/82 mmHg, repeated at 130/80. Clinical assessment finds no suspected hearing impairment; the driver follows normal conversational speech without hearing aids. The GP summary records no diabetes and no glucose-lowering medication. A maternal uncle lost vision after diabetes, which the driver initially describes as 'diabetes in the family' before clarifying that it is not his own diagnosis. There has been no personal blackout, unexplained collapse or episode of impaired awareness. The nurse keeps the current and historical eye cards separately in the record.

Synthetic prospective nurse note. No real patient data.

The driver has longstanding poor left-eye vision following an injury twelve years ago. A current ophthalmology letter records unaided right-eye acuity of 6/6 and left-eye acuity below 6/60, with no useful improvement in the left eye after refraction. Formal perimetry records a binocular horizontal field of 145 degrees; the ophthalmologist asks for a repeat field test because fixation losses were high. No confirmed new field defect is documented. The driver reports a short episode of double vision while taking a sedating medication fifteen months ago. The current eye examination records no diplopia, and that medication was stopped at the time.

The driver has continued familiar daytime delivery routes and is applying to a different employer for commercial work that includes night driving. Today's resting blood pressure readings are 128/78 and 126/80 mmHg. The nurse documents no suspected hearing loss on clinical assessment, no hearing-aid use and no difficulty following the consultation. There is no diabetes diagnosis or glucose-lowering treatment in the GP record. The driver denies spontaneous loss of consciousness, unexplained collapse or lapses of awareness while driving. The employer's older checklist labels both eyes 'normal' without acuity numbers. The driver explains that the form was completed by office staff using a previous occupational certificate rather than a new examination.

The nurse records that the driver repeatedly asks for spoken questions to be repeated when the examiner turns away. A signed audiology report provides unaided air-conduction thresholds at 500, 1000, 2000 and 3000 Hz: right ear 35, 40, 45 and 50 dB HL; left ear 45, 55, 60 and 65 dB HL. The same report describes a separate aided speech assessment, during which amplification improves recognition in quiet conditions. It does not provide an occupational driving recommendation. The driver wears hearing aids during some shifts but says the batteries have occasionally failed near the end of a long day. The workshop's environmental survey lists 82 dBA near loading equipment.

Unaided distance acuity is 6/6 in each eye. The latest optometry report documents a 150-degree binocular horizontal field, no diplopia and no monocular impairment. Blood pressure is 134/84 mmHg after rest and 132/82 on repetition. The GP record contains no diabetes diagnosis, insulin or other glucose-lowering drug. The driver denies any blackout, unexplained loss of awareness or collapse. His brother fainted after donating blood, and he clarifies that the episode did not happen to him. An employer letter states that the driver is reliable and experienced but does not describe a hearing test or a specialist assessment.

The driver reports increasing difficulty hearing a reversing alarm in a noisy depot and says conversations are easier when facing the speaker. A photocopied screening chart lists right-ear thresholds of 25, 35 and 45 dB HL at 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz, and left-ear values of 30, 40 and 50 dB HL at those frequencies. The 3000-Hz boxes are blank. There is no report of a better-ear average, and the chart does not state whether the driver was wearing the small hearing devices visible in an attached photograph. An audiology appointment is booked in three weeks. A five-year-old employer form says 'hearing pass' without a method or result.

The driver has no reported sudden unilateral change, ear pain or vertigo. Resting blood pressure is 126/80 mmHg, repeated at 128/78. Unaided acuity is 6/6 in each eye, and a recent formal eye report records a 150-degree binocular horizontal field without diplopia or monocular loss. The GP summary records no diabetes and no glucose-lowering medication. The driver describes no personal collapse, blackout or unexplained impaired awareness. His mother was assessed for recurrent dizziness; the driver supplies her condition while discussing family history, then confirms that her symptoms are not his own. The nurse records that hearing performance in the driving environment has not been measured at today's visit.

The driver describes an episode after standing for about twenty minutes in a hot collection room while fasting. He recalls nausea, sweating and dimming vision before finding himself seated on the floor. A colleague says he did not answer for about five seconds; a second witness saw him lower himself towards a chair but did not see the whole event. There was no documented tongue injury, incontinence or prolonged confusion. A capillary glucose of 5.4 mmol/L was recorded approximately thirty minutes after a sweet drink, rather than during the episode. The ECG obtained in the emergency department was reported as normal. Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is pending, and the GP has not assigned a final cause.

The episode occurred nine days before this commercial-driver assessment. The driver reports no earlier spontaneous events. His aunt has epilepsy, but he has never been given that diagnosis or antiseizure medication. Blood pressure today is 122/76 mmHg, repeated at 124/78. The optometry record documents unaided 6/6 in both eyes, a binocular horizontal field of 150 degrees and no diplopia or monocular impairment. Clinical assessment records no suspected hearing loss. There is no diabetes diagnosis or glucose-lowering treatment. The employer has asked when the driver can return to unsupervised heavy-vehicle duties; no specialist response has yet been received.

Synthetic prospective nurse note. No real patient data.

The driver reports two episodes of unexplained loss of awareness separated by ten months. The most recent was seven months ago while seated in a parked vehicle before starting a route. He recalls checking paperwork and then hearing a coworker knock on the window; he cannot account for several minutes. The earlier event occurred at home while seated. Neither account includes a reliable prodrome. A current consultant letter states that the planned cardiac and neurological investigations have been completed and that no cause has been established. The letter lists a reviewed ECG, ambulatory rhythm assessment, echocardiogram and neurological assessment; it does not supply an additional driving opinion.

The driver has not reported another episode since the last investigation and says he has been doing administrative work. His partner's separate faint after a minor injury is mentioned in conversation but is not part of his personal history. Resting blood pressure is 130/82 mmHg, repeated at 128/80. Unaided acuity is 6/6 in both eyes, with a documented 150-degree binocular horizontal field, no diplopia and no monocular loss. A clinical hearing assessment records no suspected impairment. The GP medication reconciliation records no insulin, other glucose-lowering agent or diabetes diagnosis. A previous referral form used the phrase 'investigations pending'; the consultant letter is dated later than that referral.

Synthetic prospective nurse note. No real patient data.

The driver has type 2 diabetes treated with basal and mealtime insulin. Six weeks before today's review, a coworker administered glucose while the driver was confused and unable to manage his own treatment; the contemporaneous capillary glucose was 2.7 mmol/L. The event date in the ambulance record is exactly forty-two days before the assessment date. The driver reports no later episode requiring help. His continuous-monitor download is available for most of the intervening period, but two overnight intervals are missing. An endocrinology letter from eleven months ago records early-warning symptoms and an agreed regimen; a new specialist appointment after the recent event has not yet occurred.

The driver reports awareness of a low-glucose alarm on a later occasion and treating himself while alert. The GP has not documented whether awareness or the regimen was reassessed after the assisted event. Resting blood pressure is 128/80 and 126/78 mmHg. A current eye report records unaided 6/6 in each eye, a 150-degree binocular horizontal field, no diplopia and no monocular impairment; retinal findings are described separately as absent on that examination. Clinical hearing assessment records no suspected loss. There is no other personal loss-of-awareness episode apart from the event described in the ambulance record. The employer has supplied a roster proposing long shifts with variable meal times.

Synthetic prospective nurse note. No real patient data.

The GP medication list confirms type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and a sulfonylurea, with no current insulin prescription. The driver recalls feeling shaky and hungry after missing lunch on two recent shifts. On one occasion he checked a capillary glucose of 3.7 mmol/L, drank juice and remained able to speak and care for himself. There was no witnessed loss of consciousness or assistance with treatment. A scanned emergency attendance from several years earlier mentions 'low sugar?', but contains no glucose measurement, witness account or documented need for assistance. The current GP note does not state whether hypoglycaemia awareness has been formally assessed.

During today's consultation the driver asks for questions to be repeated and says telephone conversations are difficult. No audiometry results are available, and an audiology referral is pending. He can follow speech more easily when watching the examiner's face. Resting blood pressure is 132/84 and 130/82 mmHg. Unaided acuity is 6/6 in each eye, and a recent eye report documents a 150-degree binocular horizontal field without diplopia or monocular loss; it records no driving-relevant retinal finding. The driver denies any separate unexplained collapse or period of impaired awareness. His father's insulin use appears in the family-history section of the same referral letter, while his own current treatment is listed on the medication page.

The driver attends after a depot supervisor noticed difficulty reading a distant loading-bay number and several missed spoken instructions. The nurse records blood pressure of 174/101 mmHg after five minutes seated, then 172/102 after another ten minutes. Two GP readings during the preceding week were 171/101 and 173/100. The driver has not yet started the new prescription listed in yesterday's GP letter. Today's unaided acuity is 6/9 right and 6/12 left; with spectacles it is 6/6 in both eyes. The formal binocular field result is not attached. The driver reports no double vision, and both eyes are being used.

The driver recalls an evening of fatigue after a long shift but denies losing awareness, waking on the floor or having an unexplained gap in the journey. The supervisor confirms that the driver remained responsive throughout that evening. No audiometry has been performed, and the driver relies on watching the speaker's face in a noisy room. The GP summary records no diabetes diagnosis or glucose-lowering medication; a routine fasting glucose is 5.2 mmol/L. His sister uses insulin, and her recent hypoglycaemic event was initially described while discussing family worries. The driver has not personally required assistance for low glucose. Several requested specialist appointments remain pending.

Synthetic prospective nurse note. No real patient data.

The commercial driver brings a completed GP assessment and current optometry record. Resting blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and 122/80 on repetition, consistent with the GP's 123/80 measurement last week. Unaided distance acuity is 6/6 in each eye. Formal testing records a 150-degree binocular horizontal visual field without a confirmed defect, and the optometrist documents no diplopia and no monocular impairment. Clinical hearing assessment records no suspected loss, no hearing-aid use and normal understanding of conversational instructions. The driver reports no change in hearing at work.

The GP records no personal diagnosis of diabetes and no insulin or other glucose-lowering treatment. A routine HbA1c result is 5.7 percent. The driver's brother has insulin-treated diabetes and his father had hypertension; both are listed explicitly under family history. When asked about blackouts, the driver recalls incomplete memory of recovery after a sedated dental procedure eight years ago. The dental discharge record describes planned sedation and supervised recovery. He denies spontaneous collapse, unexplained loss of consciousness, lapses of awareness during ordinary activities or unaccounted time while driving, and reports no such episode since the procedure. He takes no sedating regular medication. The nurse records the relative dates and whose history is being described without adding a driving-fitness conclusion.
